explanations.explanation: Simon of Cyrene was just passing by on his way in from the country. Then the soldiers "…forced him to carry the cross of Jesus." (Mark 15:21) Mark also tells us he was the father of Alexander and Rufus. Talk about a turn: passing by one moment, carrying the cross the next.

explanations.answer: Lead the soldiers to the hill
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think that, since Simon is a man coming in from the country. But the text never has him leading anybody. The soldiers did the forcing, and what they forced him to do was "…carry the cross of Jesus." (Mark 15:21)
No crowd control for Simon, friend. Mark doesn't give him a job like that. The soldiers forced him to carry the cross of Jesus (Mark 15:21). Simon was a man passing by on his way in from the country.

I see why that sounds possible, since they did offer it. But Mark says it plainly: they offered Him wine mixed with myrrh, "…but He did not take it." (Mark 15:23) They offered it and Jesus did not take it. So this one is False.
Yes, False. The soldiers offered Him wine mixed with myrrh, "…but He did not take it." (Mark 15:23) Mark gives no reason, so I won't make one up. All we know is what He did and didn't do at Golgotha.

Right. The soldiers divided His garments "…by casting lots to decide what each of them would take." (Mark 15:24) Each man's share came down to the lots. I think that's a hard thing to read, because those were His clothes.

Mark says nothing about guard duty here. The lots had a different job: they decided what each of the soldiers would take of His garments (Mark 15:24). So the casting of lots was about the garments, not a post to stand.

Pilate, the one who handed Jesus over to be crucified (Mark 15:15), isn't mentioned in this scene at all. The lots weren't about reports or paperwork. They were about the garments, to decide "…what each of them would take." (Mark 15:24) Nothing in the text turns this into a reporting job.
That's the one. "…the charge inscribed against Him read: THE KING OF THE JEWS." (Mark 15:26) Mark puts it right there in capital letters. It's the very charge, in the very words, written against Him.

The Son of David sounds like a big title, but Mark 15:26 doesn't use it for the charge. The charge read: THE KING OF THE JEWS. Same kind of big title, different words. Mark keeps it exact, so we do too.
Galilee does come up later in this passage, so I see how it landed in your head. But it isn't on the charge. The charge read: THE KING OF THE JEWS (Mark 15:26).

explanations.answer: Come down from the cross and save Himself
explanations.explanation: That's it. Those who passed by said, "…come down from the cross and save Yourself!" (Mark 15:30) They were shaking their heads and heaping abuse on Him as they said it (Mark 15:29). That was the dare.

explanations.answer: Call down fire from heaven on them
explanations.explanation: Nobody in this scene mentions fire, friend. What they dared Him to do was "…come down from the cross and save Yourself!" (Mark 15:30) That one is all about the cross.

explanations.answer: Tear down the temple right now
explanations.explanation: The temple does come up, and that's why this one is tricky. They mentioned it just before, saying He was going to destroy it and rebuild it in three days (Mark 15:29). But the dare itself was different: "…come down from the cross and save Yourself!" (Mark 15:30).

Yes, True. The chief priests and scribes said, "Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe!" (Mark 15:32) Mark has them saying it among themselves. That's a lot of words about believing from people who weren't believing.

This one is True, and Mark spells it out. The chief priests and scribes said, "Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross, so that we may see and believe!" (Mark 15:32) They weren't saying it to Jesus directly. They were mocking Him among themselves.

That's True. Mark says, "…even those who were crucified with Him berated Him." (Mark 15:32) That includes the two robbers on His right and left (Mark 15:27). Mark lists those passing by, the chief priests and scribes, and even the men crucified with Him.
It's actually True, friend. The verse says, "…even those who were crucified with Him berated Him." (Mark 15:32) The two robbers were crucified with Him (Mark 15:27). So even they berated Him.

Yes, darkness is the answer, baker. Mark says, "From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land." (Mark 15:33) That's three hours of it, covering all the land. Mark just states it and doesn't say more.

There's no hail in Mark's account, friend. What came over the land was darkness, not hail. Mark says, "From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land." (Mark 15:33) Hail isn't in that verse at all.

Rain would have been something you could at least carry an umbrella for. But Mark says it was darkness, not rain. "From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land." (Mark 15:33) Rain isn't mentioned in that verse.
Right. Some of those standing nearby said, "Behold, He is calling Elijah." (Mark 15:35) Jesus had cried out "Eloi, Eloi…" (Mark 15:34). Elijah is the name they gave when they heard it.
Moses is a name people know well, but Mark doesn't have the bystanders say it. They heard "Eloi, Eloi…" and said, "Behold, He is calling Elijah." (Mark 15:35) Elijah is the one they named.
Abraham never comes up in this scene. The bystanders heard "Eloi, Eloi…" and said, "Behold, He is calling Elijah." (Mark 15:35) Elijah is the one they named.
Yes, sour wine. Someone "…filled a sponge with sour wine." put it on a reed and held it up for Jesus to drink (Mark 15:36). Mark names it exactly, so we keep it exact.
Water makes sense for a sponge, I'll give you that. But Mark says the sponge was filled with sour wine (Mark 15:36). That's what was held up on the reed.

A sponge full of olive oil would be quite the mess, friend, and it isn't in Mark. The sponge was filled with sour wine and held up on a reed for Jesus to drink (Mark 15:36). Mark names sour wine, so that's what we keep.

That's right, baker. "…the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom." (Mark 15:38) Mark puts it right after Jesus breathed His last (Mark 15:37). The veil was the temple's curtain, and it tore from the top to the bottom.

I get why a robe came to mind, but Mark doesn't mention one here. At the temple, what was torn in two was the veil, "…from top to bottom." (Mark 15:38) The veil is the one thing Mark names being torn.
No scrolls get torn in Mark's account. The text says "…the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom." (Mark 15:38) That's the one thing Mark names.

I see why you'd think that, since so many others mocked Him. But Mark records the centurion saying, "Truly this man was the Son of God!" (Mark 15:39) He said it after seeing how Jesus breathed His last, and Mark doesn't record him mocking. So this one is False.

Yes, False. The centurion saw how Jesus breathed His last, and then said, "Truly this man was the Son of God!" (Mark 15:39) That wasn't mocking. After all those voices heaping abuse, his was a different one.
Yes, Mary Magdalene. Among the women watching from a distance was Mary Magdalene (Mark 15:40). Mark also names Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome.

Martha is a name you may know, the one who hosted Jesus in her home (Luke 10:38). But Mark doesn't list her among these women. The names he gives are Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome (Mark 15:40).

Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth who listened to Paul (Acts 16:14), is from a different part of the Bible. She isn't one of the women Mark names at the cross. Mark names Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome (Mark 15:40).

Yes, Galilee. These women "…had followed Jesus and ministered to Him while He was in Galilee…" (Mark 15:41) Mark also says there were many other women who had come up to Jerusalem with Him. So these women had followed Him before they stood watching.

Samaria is a real region, but Mark doesn't say that's where they followed Him. The text says they followed and ministered to Him "…while He was in Galilee…" (Mark 15:41) Galilee is the place Mark names.

Bethlehem is where Jesus was born (Matthew 2:1), so it's an understandable guess. But Mark says these women followed Jesus and ministered to Him "…while He was in Galilee…" (Mark 15:41) It's Galilee, not Bethlehem.
